title: Scorpion sting
summary: Most scorpion stings cause local pain and swelling that settle within hours. A small number of species — and young children — can have serious systemic reactions.
steps: Move the person away from where the sting happened and check no scorpion is on their clothing.
Keep the person calm and still. Lay them down with the stung limb still and supported.
Wash the sting site with soap and clean water.
Apply a cool compress wrapped in a cloth for 10–15 minutes at a time to ease pain and swelling.
An adult dose of paracetamol can ease pain. Avoid aspirin if the person is under 18.
Watch carefully for the next several hours: difficulty breathing, drooling, muscle twitching, sweating, vomiting, fast heartbeat, or restlessness — any of these means immediate hospital care.
avoid: Do not cut the sting site or try to suck out the venom.
Do not apply ice directly to the skin.
Do not give alcohol, sedatives, or strong pain medicines that mask new symptoms.
whenToEscalate: Any sting in a child, elderly person, or someone with heart, lung, or pregnancy concerns — see a doctor the same day.
Emergency immediately for: difficulty breathing or swallowing, drooling, muscle twitching, blurred vision, fast or irregular heartbeat, severe sweating, vomiting, collapse, or loss of consciousness.
Severe local pain not eased by paracetamol and a cool compress, or rapid spreading swelling.
Any sting where the scorpion is known to be a medically important species in your region.
specialty: Emergency department for any systemic symptoms; general physician for review.
